# Overview

This project explores how pest-control service activity varied across Seattle Neighborhoods and seasons in 2023. Using R, spatial joins, and interactive bipartite graphs, I turned service records into a view of which pest categories were most common and where those services occurred.

A service record may represent a confirmed issue, a suspected problem, or preventative treatment, not necessarily a pest sighting.

# Data Overview

This analysis combines more than 30,000 service records from a local Seattle pest-control company with neighborhood boundary data from the Seattle City GIS Open Data Portal. The fields below are the primary variables used in the analysis. To protect customer privacy, individual addresses and coordinate values are not included in the published project.

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Date` | Service date. |
| `Season` | Winter, spring, summer, or fall, derived from the service month. |
| `Target` | Recorded pest label, consolidated into broader categories. |
| `Address` | Service address, used for the Seattle filter and original geocoding. |
| `Latitude`, `Longitude` | Coordinates used to assign service locations to neighborhoods. |
| `Neighborhood` | One of seven Seattle neighborhoods defined for this project. |
| `L_HOOD`, `S_HOOD`, `S_HOOD_ALT` | Neighborhood, sub-neighborhood, and alternate names from the boundary layer; `S_HOOD` is used for larger Neighborhood grouping. |

**Nodes:** two sets—pest categories and the seven broader Seattle neighborhoods.  
**Edges:** connections between a pest category and a neighborhood, weighted by the number of service records.

# Import and Preparation

The workflow uses `readxl` for data import, `tidyverse` and `lubridate` for data preparation, `tidygeocoder` and `sf` for geocoding and spatial analysis, and `bipartiteD3` with `RColorBrewer` for interactive network visualization.

```{r setup, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide', include=FALSE}
# installing packages if needed (uncomment to run)

```


## Reading the Data

The Excel workbook is read into R and filtered to only include Seattle addresses. This excerpt shows the import and filter; the working local directory settings are kept out of the displayed code.

```r
# reading the service workbook
sea_pests <- read_excel("sea_pests.xlsx")

sea_pests <- sea_pests %>%
  filter(grepl("Seattle", Address, ignore.case = TRUE))
```

```{r data-import, include=FALSE}
# setting our working directory and reading the data
setwd("removed")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = getwd())

# filtering to only include Seattle addresses

  filter(grepl("Seattle", Address, ignore.case = TRUE))
```

## Geocoding Addresses

I used `tidygeocoder` to obtain latitude and longitude from service addresses so the records could be assigned to neighborhoods.

```{r geocoding, echo=TRUE}
# creating a new variable called 'coordinates' that takes the addresses and
# uses tidygeocoder to convert them to lat/long coordinates

sea_pests$coordinates <- tidygeocoder::geo(sea_pests$Address)

# renaming columns for clarity and only keeping the necessary ones
sea_pests <- sea_pests %>%
  # mutate(Latitude = coordinates$lat,
         # Longitude = coordinates$long) %>%
  select(Date, Target, Latitude, Longitude)
```

```{r geocoding-verify, echo=TRUE}
# show column names to make sure the new columns were added and named correctly
colnames(sea_pests)
```


## Dates and Seasons

Service dates are parsed with `mdy()`, then assigned to winter (December–February), spring (March–May), summer (June–August), or fall (September–November). Winter combines the winter months within the 2023 calendar year.

```{r data-cleaning, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# converting service dates to a consistent date format
sea_pests <- sea_pests %>%
  mutate(Date = mdy(Date))

# assigning a season based on the service month
sea_pests <- sea_pests %>%
  mutate(Season = case_when(
    month(Date) %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "Winter",
    month(Date) %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ "Spring",
    month(Date) %in% c(6, 7, 8) ~ "Summer",
    month(Date) %in% c(9, 10, 11) ~ "Fall",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))
```


```{r data-cleaning-verify, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# checking for missing values before continuing
sum(is.na(sea_pests))
```

```{r data-clean-verify, include=FALSE}
# checking that our date is formatted and our season column was created
sea_pests %>% slice_head(n = 1)
```


# Pest-Category Grouping

Pest labeling was not standardized, so related labels were consolidated into broader categories. This makes the graphs easier to compare while reducing detail within each group.

| Category                     | Types                                                                 |
|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Ants**                     | Carpenter, Nuisance, Pavement, Odorous House, Moisture, and other Misc/General Ants |
| **Rodents**                  | Mice, Rats, Misc. Vertebrates     |
| **Cockroaches**              | General, German, American, and Oriental Cockroaches |
| **Biting Insects**           | Bed Bugs, Fleas, Mites                                                |
| **Storage and Structure Pests** | Fabric Pests (moths, carpet beetles), Food Storage Pests (non wood-destroying storage beetles, weevils), Wood-Destroying Beetles, Termites     |
| **Stinging Insects**         | Wasps, Hornets                                                       |
| **Spiders**                  | General Spiders                                                      |
| **Flying Insects**           | House, Fruit, and Drain Flies. Other Misc general non-stinging Flying Insects                                  |
| **Misc Crawling Insects**    | Silverfish, Stinkbugs, Other Crawling Insects                        |

```{r pest-grouping, include=FALSE}

# the names used below to create the broader groups are based on the original pest types that are manually logged when completing a service. These are documented by technicians while they are on site and are, unfortunately, not standardized.
sea_pests <- sea_pests %>%
  mutate(Target = case_when(
    Target %in% c("Ants - Carpenter", "Ants - Nuisance", "Ants - Pavement", 
                  "Ants", "Ants - Crawling Insects", "Ants - Odorous", 
                  "Ants - Moisture", "Ants _ Ants", "Ants - General Ants") ~ "Ants",
    Target %in% c("Rodents - Mice", "Rodents - Rats", "Rodents", "Vertebrate", 
                  "Vertebrate - Large", "Vertebrate - Small", "Vertebrate - General",
                  "Rodents, Rodents - Mice, Rodents - Rats", "Rodents, Rodents - Mice", 
                  "Rodents - Mice, Rodents - Rats", "Rodents - General") ~ "Rodents",
    Target %in% c("Flies - House", "Flying Insects", 
                  "Flying Insects, General insect control") ~ "Flying Insects",
    Target %in% c("Biting Insects - Bed Bugs", "Biting Insects - Fleas", 
                  "Biting Insects - Mites", 
                  "Biting Insects, Biting Insects - Bed Bugs", "Biting Insects, Biting Insects - Fleas", 
                  "Biting Insects - Bed Bugs, General insect control", 
                  "Biting Insects - Fleas, General insect control", 
                  "Biting Insects - Fleas, General insect control, Bed Bugs") ~ "Biting Insects",
    Target %in% c("Stinging Insects", "Wasps", "General insect control, Stinging Insects", 
                  "Stinging Insects, General insect control", "Hornets", 
                  "Hornet - Stinging Insect") ~ "Stinging Insects",
    Target %in% c("Fabric Pests", "Food Storage Pests", "WDO - Beetles", 
                  "WDO - Termites", "Fabric Pests, General insect control", 
                  "Food Storage Pests, General insect control") ~ "Storage and Structure Pests",
    Target == "Cockroaches" ~ "Cockroaches",
    Target == "Spiders" ~ "Spiders",
    TRUE ~ Target  # Do not change other entries
  ))
```


```{r pest-grouping-verify, include=FALSE}
# creating a table to show the counts of each pest category to peep the distribution
sea_pests %>%
  group_by(Target) %>%
  summarise(Count = n(), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  arrange(desc(Count))
```


# Neighborhood Grouping

I downloaded the Seattle sub-neighborhood boundary shapefile from the [Seattle City GIS open data portal](https://data-seattlecitygis.opendata.arcgis.com/datasets/b4a142f592e94d39a3bf787f3c112c1d/explore). Figure 1 (below) comes from the same portal and provides a reference for the boundaries used to assign service locations to neighborhoods.

  <img src="seattle_map.png"
       alt="Seattle Sub-Neighborhoods Map"
       style="width: 40%; height: auto;"/>

  <p><em>Figure 1. Seattle Sub-Neighborhoods.</em></p>
</div>

## Assigning Service Locations to Sub-Neighborhoods

The downloaded boundaries were transformed to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to match the geocoded service coordinates. I then converted the service locations to spatial points and used `st_within()` in a spatial join to identify the sub-neighborhood containing each point.

```{r neighborhood-grouping, echo=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# reading the neighborhood boundaries downloaded from the Seattle GIS portal
neighborhoods <- sf::st_read("Neighborhood_Map_Atlas_Neighborhoods.shp")

# checking the coordinate reference systems before the spatial join
st_crs(sea_pests)  # coordinates are assigned a CRS when converted to sf
st_crs(neighborhoods)  # 2926

# transforming the neighborhood boundaries to match the service coordinates
neighborhoods <- st_transform(neighborhoods, crs = 4326)

# converting service coordinates to spatial points
pest_sf <- st_as_sf(sea_pests, coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326)

# assigning service points to the neighborhoods they fall within
pest_neighborhoods <- st_join(pest_sf, neighborhoods, join = st_within)
```

```{r neighborhood-grouping-verify, include=FALSE}
# checking the join without displaying individual service locations
head(pest_neighborhoods)
```

## Grouping Sub-Neighborhoods into Neighborhoods

To keep the network graphs readable, I grouped the sub-neighborhoods into seven broader neighborhoods/regions based on geographic proximity. These groupings were created for this project and are not official administrative units.

```{r neighborhood-grouping-continue, include=FALSE}

# defining the seven regional groupings
get_custom_segment <- function(neighborhood) {
  if (neighborhood %in% c("Loyal Heights", "Ballard", "Whittier Heights", 
                          "West Woodland", "Phinney Ridge", "Wallingford", 
                          "Fremont", "Green Lake", "Broadview", "Bitter Lake", 
                          "Haller Lake", "North Beach/Blue Ridge", "Licton Springs", 
                          "Crown Hill", "Greenwood", "Sunset Hill")) {
    return("NW Seattle")
  } else if (neighborhood %in% c("View Ridge", "Ravenna", "Sand Point", "Bryant", 
                                 "Windermere", "Laurelhurst", "Roosevelt", 
                                 "University of Washington", "Wedgwood", 
                                 "Victory Heights", "Matthews Beach", "Meadowbrook", 
                                 "Olympic Hills", "Cedar Park", "Pinehurst", 
                                 "Maple Leaf", "University District", 
                                 "University Heights")) {
    return("NE Seattle")
  } else if (neighborhood %in% c("East Queen Anne", "West Queen Anne", 
                                 "Lower Queen Anne", "North Queen Anne", 
                                 "Westlake", "Lawton Park", "Briarcliff", 
                                 "Southeast Magnolia", "Interbay")) {
    return("Magnolia/Queen Anne")
  } else if (neighborhood %in% c("Eastlake", "Madrona", "Harrison/Denny-Blaine", 
                                 "Minor", "Leschi", "Mann", "First Hill", 
                                 "Yesler Terrace", "Portage Bay", "Montlake", 
                                 "Madison Park", "Broadway", "Stevens")) {
    return("Central Seattle")
  } else if (neighborhood %in% c("South Lake Union", "Pike-Market", "Belltown", 
                                 "International District", "Central Business District", 
                                 "Pioneer Square", "Denny Triangle")) {
    return("Downtown Seattle")
  } else if (neighborhood %in% c("South Park", "Seaview", "Gatewood", 
                                 "Arbor Heights", "Alki", "North Admiral", 
                                 "Fairmount Park", "Genesee", "Fauntleroy", 
                                 "Highland Park", "North Delridge", "Riverview", 
                                 "High Point", "South Delridge", "Roxhill")) {
    return("West Seattle")
  } else if (neighborhood %in% c("Atlantic", "SODO", "Georgetown", 
                                 "North Beacon Hill", "Mid-Beacon Hill", 
                                 "South Beacon Hill", "Holly Park", "Brighton", 
                                 "Dunlap", "Rainier Beach", "Rainier View", 
                                 "Mount Baker", "Columbia City", "Seward Park", 
                                 "Industrial District", "Harbor Island")) {
    return("South/SE Seattle")
  } else {
    return(NA)
  }
}

# assigning each sub-neighborhood to its project-defined larger neighborhood
pest_neighborhoods <- pest_neighborhoods %>%
  mutate(Neighborhood = sapply(S_HOOD, get_custom_segment))
```

```{r neighborhood-grouping-verify-2, include=FALSE}
# checking the region assignments 
head(pest_neighborhoods)
```

The mapping function uses the shapefile's `S_HOOD` field to assign each record to a region.


```r
# assigning each sub-neighborhood to its project-defined larger neighborhood
pest_neighborhoods <- pest_neighborhoods %>%
  mutate(Neighborhood = sapply(S_HOOD, get_custom_segment))
```

# Bipartite Graphs and Analysis

Bipartite graphs connect two different sets of nodes — here, pest categories and Seattle regions. I chose to use Bipartite graphs because they show both the overall mix of services and the regional connections for each pest category in one view. Wider connections represent more service records.

## Preparing the Graph Data

After assigning neighborhoods and regions, the data is still stored as an sf object containing spatial geometry. To prepare it for the network visualizations, I remove the geometry, convert it to a regular data frame, and keep the four relevant fields: Date, Season, Target, and Neighborhood.

```{r bipartite-data-prep, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
# dropping geometry and keeping the fields used in the network
sea_pests_df <- as.data.frame(st_drop_geometry(pest_neighborhoods)) %>%
  select(Date, Season, Target, Neighborhood)
```

## Reusable Network Function

The function optionally filters to one season, counts records by pest category and region, and reshapes those counts into a matrix. Categories and regions are ordered by total frequency. The matrix supplies the weighted connections for `bipartite_D3()`.

Using the same function for every period keeps the aggregation and chart settings consistent.

A custom color palette using `RColorBrewer's` Paired palette was also created so consistent coloring can be used for each pest category across all five graphs.

```{r bipartite-colors, include=FALSE}

# custom colors using RColorBrewer's Paired palette
paired_colors <- brewer.pal(12, "Paired")

# manually selecting colors
custom_colors <- c(
  "Ants" = paired_colors[1],
  "Rodents" = paired_colors[3],
  "Cockroaches" = paired_colors[5],
  "Biting Insects" = paired_colors[4],
  "Spiders" = paired_colors[10],
  "Flying Insects" = paired_colors[9],
  "Storage and Structure Pests" = paired_colors[7],
  "Stinging Insects" = paired_colors[8],
  "Misc Crawling Insects" = paired_colors[6]
)
```

```{r bipartite-function, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# building the annual or seasonal graph with the same settings
create_bipartiteD3_graph <- function(data, season = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(season)) {
    # filtering to the selected season
    data <- data %>% filter(Season == season)
  }
  
  # counting service records and arranging them in a pest-by-region matrix
  sightings_matrix <- data %>%
    group_by(Target, Neighborhood) %>%
    summarise(Sightings = n(), .groups = 'drop') %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = Neighborhood, values_from = Sightings, values_fill = 0) %>%
    column_to_rownames("Target") %>%
    as.matrix()
  
  # sorting pest categories by total service count
  sort_primary <- data %>%
    group_by(Target) %>%
    summarise(Total = n(), .groups = 'drop') %>%
    arrange(desc(Total)) %>%
    pull(Target)
  
  # sorting neighborhoods by total service count
  sort_secondary <- data %>%
    group_by(Neighborhood) %>%
    summarise(Total = n(), .groups = 'drop') %>%
    arrange(desc(Total)) %>%
    pull(Neighborhood)
  
  # creating bipartite graph using bipartiteD3 with custom colors
  bipartite_D3(
    sightings_matrix, 
    PrimaryLab = "Pest Type", 
    SecondaryLab = "Neighborhood", 
    SiteNames = if (is.null(season)) "Bipartite Graph of Seattle Pest Services in 2023" else paste("Bipartite Graph of Seattle Pest Services in", season, "2023"),
    SortPrimary = sort_primary,
    SortSecondary = sort_secondary,
    colouroption = "manual",
    NamedColourVector = custom_colors,
    ColourBy = 1,
    PercentageDecimals = 2,
    MainFigSize = c(800, 475),      
    IndivFigSize = c(200, 400),     
    BoxLabPos = c(35, 35),          
    PercPos = c(240, 210),          
    MinWidth = 0,                   
    Pad = 8                         
  )
}

```


# Full-Year and Seasonal Results

**Hover over a *Pest Type* or *Neighborhood* to inspect its connections.**


Connection widths represent service-record counts. Percentages describe the displayed *service distribution*, not the proportion of Seattle properties affected. 

## Full Year: 2023

```{r bipartite-graph-entire-year, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align='center'}

# creating a bipartite graph for the entire year
create_bipartiteD3_graph(sea_pests_df)
```


Rodents accounted for **46.78%** of annual records, followed by ants (**31.23%**) and cockroaches (**15.74%**). Rodent services were prominent in South/SE and Central Seattle, ants had a strong West Seattle connection, and cockroach services were concentrated in Downtown and South/SE Seattle.

## Winter

```{r bipartite-graph-winter, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align='center'}

# creating bipartite graphs for each season
create_bipartiteD3_graph(sea_pests_df, season = "Winter")

```


Rodents represented **54.58%** of winter records, followed by ants (**21.80%**) and cockroaches (**18.59%**). Winter had the highest rodent share of the four seasons.

## Spring

```{r bipartite-graph-spring, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align='center'}

create_bipartiteD3_graph(sea_pests_df, season = "Spring")

```


Rodents remained the largest category (**46.52%**), while the ant share increased to **35.79%**. Cockroaches accounted for **13.93%**.

## Summer

```{r bipartite-graph-summer, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align='center'}

create_bipartiteD3_graph(sea_pests_df, season = "Summer")

```


Ants became the leading category (**40.45%**), narrowly exceeding rodents (**39.80%**). Cockroaches accounted for **13.23%**. This was the only season in which ants surpassed rodents.

## Fall

```{r bipartite-graph-fall, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align='center'}

create_bipartiteD3_graph(sea_pests_df, season = "Fall")

```


Rodents returned to the largest share (**47.21%**), followed by ants (**25.83%**) and cockroaches (**17.52%**). West Seattle remained a prominent region for ant services, while Downtown remained prominent for cockroach services.

# Conclusions and Limitations

## Main Takeaways

The graphs show which pest categories accounted for the most service activity and how those services were distributed across Seattle in 2023. Rodents led in every season except summer, when ants had the largest share. Ant services had a strong West Seattle connection, while cockroach services were concentrated in Downtown Seattle.

Combining geographic assignment with a two-mode network made these regional and seasonal relationships easier to explore than separate category totals alone.

## Limitations

Interpretation is limited by:

* service demand and preventive contracts rather than a random sample of pest presence
* repeat visits and customer mix
* inconsistent technician-entered labels and broad category consolidation
* geocoding quality, spatial-join misses, and region definitions created for this analysis
* a single company's Seattle service records from 2023
* interactive-package constraints on labels, layout, and customization

These results are descriptive. They should not be used as citywide prevalence estimates or causal claims.

## Data Sources

**Service records:** Proprietary 2023 data from a local pest-control company. The company is not identified, and the underlying records are not publicly shared.

**Neighborhood boundaries and reference map:** City of Seattle, Office of Planning and Community Development. *Neighborhood Map Atlas—Neighborhoods* (cityclerk_nma_nhoods) [GIS dataset]. Derived from the Seattle City Clerk’s Office Geographic Indexing Atlas. Available through the [Seattle City GIS Open Data Portal](https://data-seattlecitygis.opendata.arcgis.com/datasets/b4a142f592e94d39a3bf787f3c112c1d/explore). Metadata updated December 1, 2020.
